summary:
HEXATOUR is a free website that lets students explore the worlds NASA robots have visited. Visitors slide through nine stops, from Mercury to deep space, in a 2D or 3D view, and tap planets, asteroids and spacecraft to open fact cards. Each world lists the real robots that went there, 25 in all, and each robot has its own page with its launch date, status, timeline, findings, people and NASA source links.

The problem we address is that NASA mission facts are spread across many pages written for experts, so students struggle to see which robot went where. HEXATOUR puts them in one place at three learning levels. Cadet gives a short briefing, audio and fun facts. Astronaut adds planetary science notes, a quiz and orbit paths. Commander adds an astrophysics report, telemetry tables and a gravity lab.

Planet data comes from the NASA planetary fact sheets. Mission facts, photos and distances come from NASA Science, the NASA Image and Video Library and NASA/JPL Horizons.
details: We used Claude Code, an AI coding assistant from Anthropic, to help build HEXATOUR. It wrote and revised much of the website code (the React interface, the 3D views, the learning levels and the layout), and it helped us prepare the project presentation and this submission text. Planet maps, spacecraft photos and all scientific data come from NASA sources, not from AI generation. The spacecraft models and the Uranus surface are drawn by code, and the site says so. No AI image generation was used. Our team chose the project idea, direction and requirements, and reviewed the results.
